title: Valid Parenthesis String
pattern: greedy over the range of reachable open-bracket counts
statement:
A bracket string is built from three characters: `(`, `)` and `*`. A `*` is a wildcard and may stand for a `(`, for a `)`, or for nothing at all.

Given such a string `s`, decide whether some way of replacing every `*` turns `s` into a valid bracket sequence, meaning every `)` is matched by an earlier `(` and no `(` is left without a partner.

Return `true` if such a replacement exists, and `false` otherwise.

Example: `s = "(*))"` is `true`, because the `*` can become `(`. `s = "((*"` is `false`, since after replacing the `*` there are still three opens and at most one close. `s = ")*"` is `false`, because the leading `)` can never be matched.

Constraints: `1 <= s.length <= 100` and every character of `s` is one of `(`, `)` or `*`.

constraints: Inputs are JSON-serializable values satisfying the bounds stated above.
hints: You do not have to choose a meaning for each `*` right now. Instead, after each prefix ask which numbers of open brackets are still reachable.
That set of reachable open counts is always a contiguous range: `(` and `)` shift it by one, `*` widens it by one at each end. Two numbers therefore describe everything.

A prefix is already impossible when even the smallest reachable count is below zero. At the end the smallest reachable count must be exactly 0, because a string is not valid while an open bracket is still waiting.

editorial.approach: The brute force is interval dynamic programming. A valid bracket sequence is a concatenation of matched blocks, so `possible(i, j)` is true either when `s[i]` is a `*` used as nothing and `possible(i + 1, j)` holds, or when `s[i]` (a `(` or a `*`) matches some later position `k - 1` (a `)` or a `*`), which leaves the inside `possible(i + 1, k - 1)` and the tail `possible(k, j)` to be valid in turn. Every interval is filled in order of increasing length, giving O(n²) states and O(n) work per state. The optimal never decides what a `*` means. It tracks the interval `[lo, hi]` of how many brackets could be open after the prefix read so far: `(` raises both, `)` lowers both, and `*` lowers the minimum (it may be a `)`) while raising the maximum (it may be a `(`). If the maximum ever goes negative the prefix cannot be fixed, and the minimum is floored at 0, because a prefix never needs to close more brackets than it has opened.
editorial.why_optimal: The reachable set of open counts after a prefix is always a contiguous range, so those two integers describe it completely and a single left-to-right pass suffices; every character must be examined at least once, making O(n) optimal. The final answer depends on the minimum being exactly 0, not the maximum: the string may end with fewer opens than the wildcards allowed, but it must not be forced to leave an open bracket unmatched. The O(n³) DP is legal at n <= 100 but is roughly 10^4 times slower than the counters.
editorial.pitfalls: Testing only `hi === 0` at the end is wrong, since a shorter final count is also reachable; the condition is `lo === 0` while `hi` never went below zero. The minimum must be floored at 0 and not allowed to go negative, otherwise a run of `*` used as `)` incorrectly kills the string. A prefix whose maximum dips below 0 must return false immediately (`hi -= 1` before the check, and return as soon as `hi < 0`), because the extra `)` can never be matched. In the DP, a lone `*` is valid (it can be empty), so the length-one interval needs its own base case; forgetting it makes `"*"` come out false. Empty strings are valid and must return true.
